query: Should our intervention target all pregnant women for anemia prevention or only women with Hb <11 g/dL; what are the operational, ethical, and measurement implications of each choice?

response.query: Should our intervention target all pregnant women for anemia prevention or only women with Hb <11 g/dL; what are the operational, ethical, and measurement implications of each choice?
response.answer: Targeting all pregnant women for anemia prevention may be costlier but ensures no one is missed. Targeting only women with Hb <11 g/dL focuses resources but risks overlooking those with mild anemia. Ethically, universal screening may be preferred to avoid bias.

results.content: Phil Rosen Award for the Best Abstract on Clinical or Epidemiology Research by a Trainee 7 Effectiveness of the Making it Work™ Program at Improving Presenteeism and Work Cessation in Workers with Inflammatory Arthritis – Results of a Randomized Controlled Trial Andre Luquini (University of British Columbia - Department of Experimental Medicine / Arthritis Research Canada, Richmond); Yufei Zheng (Arthritis Research Canada, Richmond); Hui Xie (Arthritis Research Canada/Faculty of Health Sciences at Simon Fraser University, Richmond); Catherine Backman (Rehab Sciences/Occupational Therapy, University of British Columbia, Richmond); Pamela Rogers (Arthritis Research Canada, Richmond); Alex Kwok (Arthritis Research Canada, Richmond); Astrid Knight (Arthritis Research Canada, Richmond); Monique Gignac (Institute for Work and Health, Dalla Lana School of Public Health, University of Toronto, Toronto); Dianne Mosher (University of Calgary, Calgary); Linda Li (Rehab Sciences/Physical Therapy, University of British Columbia, Arthritis Research Canada, Richmond); John Esdaile (University of British Columbia (Division of Rheumatology)/Arthritis Research Canada, Richmond); Carter Thorne (University of Toronto (Division of Rheumatology) / Southlake Regional Health Centre, Newmarket); Diane Lacaille (University of British Columbia (Division of Rheumatology)/ Arthritis Research Canada, Richmond) Objectives: Arthritis often leads to presenteeism (decreased at-work productivity) and permanent work disability, the worst occupational outcome of a disease, leading to reduced quality of life and cost to society.
